1a.html:
Mn alone resists graphitisation and promotes pearlite (slides 4, 6; book p 296):

  • It dissolves in cementite as (\mathrm{Fe,Mn})_3\mathrm{C} and stabilises it, so it promotes chill and carbide.
  • In austenite it raises the carbon solubility and the combined carbon, lowers the eutectoid (austenitising) temperature and raises hardenability. The austenite then transforms to pearlite instead of ferrite + graphite, and the pearlite is finer.
  • Excess Mn segregates to the last-freezing cell boundaries, forms intercellular carbides and retards tempering (slide 15).

Mn with S (the main interaction). S in the melt forms FeS, which promotes cementite. Mn has a higher affinity for S and forms MnS, which separates early as harmless, randomly placed particles. So Mn first cancels the FeS (acting, in effect, as a graphitiser), and only the excess Mn acts as above:

Mn, wt%Effect
1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}stoichiometric MnS, no effect on the microstructure
1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15maximum ferrite, minimum pearlite
3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35pearlitic microstructure

Mn with other elements.

  • Si, the graphitiser, opposes Mn, so the matrix is set by the balance of Si against free Mn.
  • Cu, Ni and Sn add to its pearlite-promoting effect (pearlitic grades, heavy sections). With Cr the carbide effect adds up, giving chilled or white iron.
  • In ductile iron, Mg removes the S, so nearly all the Mn is free; it segregates and forms carbides, so ferritic grades keep Mn low.
pts: Mn alone stabilises cementite, (\mathrm{Fe,Mn})_3\mathrm{C}, and resists graphitisation (chill, carbides)
Mn alone raises carbon solubility and combined carbon, lowers the eutectoid temperature and raises hardenability: pearlite promoter, finer pearlite
Excess Mn segregates to cell boundaries: intercellular carbides, slower tempering
With S: FeS promotes cementite; MnS forms first; gives the 1.7S, 1.7S + 0.15 and 3S + 0.35 rules with their effects
With other elements: Si opposes it; Cu and Ni reinforce pearlite; Cr adds carbide; in Mg-treated ductile iron Mn is free and forms carbides
1a.src: Ch 6 Cast Iron, slides 4-6, 15; Heat Treatment of Ferrous Alloys (course book), pp 294, 296, 306; Standard textbook treatment
1a.watch:
• The factor 1.7 is the Mn to S mass ratio in MnS: 54.94/32.06 = 1.71.
  • Do not call Mn simply a graphitiser or simply a carbide former. The question's point is that its effect depends on how much S it must first neutralise.

1b.html:
Given: grey iron cylinder, D = 20 in, L = 50 in; 3.5% C (2.2\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}), 1.8% Si (3.21\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}), 0.035% S (2.07\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}); Mn density 7.21\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

Find: the minimum Mn for a fully pearlitic structure on normalising, as wt% and as mass.

Assumptions: a solid cylinder; the balance is Fe (7.87\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}); P and other elements negligible; no Mn in the base iron and 100% recovery; volumes additive.

Step 1. Mn requirement (slide 4). Mn first combines with S as MnS, which removes the cementite-promoting FeS; only the excess Mn stabilises pearlite. The S-Mn rules give:

\begin{aligned} 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} &= 1.7(0.035) = 0.06\% \quad (\text{MnS only, no effect}) \\ 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15 &= 0.21\% \quad (\text{maximum ferrite}) \\ 3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35 &= 3(0.035) + 0.35 = 0.455\% \quad (\text{pearlitic}) \end{aligned}

The minimum for a pearlitic matrix is therefore 0.455 wt% Mn.

Step 2. Composition: \mathrm{Fe} = 100 - 3.5 - 1.8 - 0.035 - 0.455 = 94.21 wt%.

Step 3. Density (inverse rule of mixtures):

\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\rho} &= \sum \frac{w_i}{\rho_i} = \frac{0.035}{2.2} + \frac{0.018}{3.21} + \frac{0.00035}{2.07} + \frac{0.00455}{7.21} + \frac{0.9421}{7.87} \\ &= 0.01591 + 0.00561 + 0.00017 + 0.00063 + 0.11971 = 0.14202\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}} \\ \rho &= 7.04\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} \end{aligned}

This is a normal value for grey iron (about 7.0 to 7.2\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}): the light graphite brings it below steel.

Step 4. Volume:

\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L = \frac{\pi}{4}(20)^2(50) = 15{,}708\ \mathrm{in^3} \\ &= 15{,}708 \times 16.387\ \mathrm{cm^3\,in^{-3}} = 2.574 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{cm^3}\ (0.257\ \mathrm{m^3}) \end{aligned}

Step 5. Mass:

m = \rho V = 7.041 \times 2.574 \times 10^5 = 1.812 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{g} = 1812\ \mathrm{kg}

Step 6. Mn needed:

m_{\mathrm{Mn}} = 0.00455 \times 1812 = 8.25\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{Mn}} = \frac{8246\ \mathrm{g}}{7.21\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}} \approx 1144\ \mathrm{cm^3}

Answer: at least 0.455 wt% Mn, that is about 8.25 kg of Mn (about 1140\ \mathrm{cm^3}) for the 1.81 t casting. Any Mn already in the charge is subtracted. Added as 75% ferromanganese with 90% recovery, it is about 12.2 kg of alloy.

Normalising link. Normalise at 885 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C} for about 1 h per inch of section (about 20 h here), then cool in still air or with fans (slides 8, 12). The centre of so heavy a section cools slowly and would form ferrite next to the flakes. The full pearlitic Mn level, with 0.4 to 0.8% Cu if needed, keeps it pearlitic.
pts: Explains that Mn first ties up S as MnS (FeS promotes cementite) and only the excess Mn promotes pearlite
Applies the pearlitic rule: \mathrm{Mn} = 3(0.035) + 0.35 = 0.455 wt%, compared with 0.06% (MnS only) and 0.21% (maximum ferrite)
States the assumptions: Fe balance 94.21 wt% at 7.87\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}, solid cylinder, no Mn in the base iron, full recovery
Density by the inverse rule of mixtures: 0.1420\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}}, so \rho = 7.04\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}
Volume 15{,}708\ \mathrm{in^3} = 2.574 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{cm^3}, with the unit conversion shown
Casting mass about 1812 kg
Final answer: Mn mass about 8.25 kg (about 1140\ \mathrm{cm^3})
Practical addition: subtract the Mn already in the charge; allow for ferromanganese grade and recovery (about 12 kg of 75% FeMn)
Normalising link: 885 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 1 h per inch (about 20 h), air or fan cooling; the heavy section needs the full pearlitic Mn level
1b.src: Ch 6 Cast Iron, slides 4, 6, 8, 12; Heat Treatment of Ferrous Alloys (course book), pp 294, 296-297
1b.watch:
• The printed Si density (3.21\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}, which is the density of SiC) is above the true value (2.33\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}). It is used as printed. With 2.33 the density becomes 6.94\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} and the Mn 8.1 kg, so the answer barely changes.
  • Do not answer with 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} (0.06%): that only neutralises the S. 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15 maximises ferrite, the opposite of what is asked.
  • Do not average the densities by weight (\sum w_i \rho_i). Mass fractions combine through specific volumes, 1/\rho = \sum w_i/\rho_i.
  • "Amount" is read as the mass of Mn to add. If the examiner wanted only the wt%, the 0.455% line carries those marks.

2a.html:
Grade (class) 4 is the medium- to high-alloy hot-work tool steel, for example H13 (about 0.4C-5Cr-1.3Mo-1V). Its low carbon gives lath martensite and a lower as-quenched hardness (about 52 HRC) than high-speed steel, but it shows the same secondary hardening (slide 27).

Three effects act together (slide 28):

  1. Up to about 400^\circ\mathrm{C}: \varepsilon-carbide, then cementite films, form in and between the laths; carbon leaves the martensite and dislocations recover. Hardness falls slightly.
  2. About 450 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C}: Cr, Mo and V diffuse and replace cementite by ultrafine coherent \mathrm{M_2C} and VC on the lath dislocations, and the small amount of retained austenite becomes fresh martensite on cooling. These offset the softening and give a mild secondary hump near 550^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  3. Above about 600^\circ\mathrm{C}: the carbides coarsen (to \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} and \mathrm{M_6C}) at lath and prior-austenite boundaries and the matrix recovers: hardness falls steeply.

The synergism: hardness = softening of martensite + precipitation hardening + transformed austenite. With less carbon and retained austenite than class 3, the hump is small. Hot-work dies are double tempered above it, about 540 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 44 to 52 HRC), for toughness and so they do not soften in service.
pts: Identifies grade 4 as medium- to high-alloy hot-work steel (H13 type): low-carbon lath martensite, lower starting hardness
Schematic: lower start, near plateau, mild hump near 550 degrees C, steep fall above 600 degrees C, with the component curves
Low temperature: \varepsilon-carbide then cementite, carbon leaves martensite, recovery, slight softening
450 to 550 degrees C: ultrafine coherent \mathrm{M_2C} and VC precipitate on dislocations (secondary hardening)
Retained austenite becomes fresh martensite on cooling
Above 600 degrees C: carbides coarsen on boundaries, matrix recovers, steep fall
States the synergism (sum of softening and the two hardening effects) and the practice: double temper at about 540 to 620 degrees C
2a.sketch:
• Hardness (HRC) against tempering temperature (0 to 700 degrees C): class 4 curve starting near 52 HRC, almost flat with a slight fall to about 400 degrees C, a small hump near 550 degrees C, a steep fall above 600 degrees C; the class 3 curve above it for comparison is optional.
  • Under it, the three component curves of slide 28: martensite softening (falling), retained-austenite transformation (rising from about 450 degrees C), carbide precipitation (rising above 500 degrees C).
  • Three micro-sketches: as-quenched lath martensite; laths with very fine needle-like alloy carbide at 550 degrees C; recovered ferrite with coarse carbides on the boundaries at 650 degrees C.
2a.src: Ch 4 Tool Steels, slides 11, 25-29; Heat Treatment of Ferrous Alloys (course book), pp 254-259; Standard textbook treatment
2a.watch:
• "Grade 4" is read as class 4 of slide 27 (hot-work tool steels). If the high-speed class was meant, the same three-effect explanation applies, with a higher start and a peak above the as-quenched hardness.
  • "With the help of its microstructures" needs the phases at each stage named (and sketched), not only the curve.
  • The HRC values are typical of H13, not from the slides.

2b.html:
Given: as quenched, 60 HRC with 80% martensite and 20% retained austenite (RA, 40 HRC). After cryotreatment and three tempers at 550^\circ\mathrm{C}: 2% RA and 68 HRC; martensite formed from RA 65 HRC; the initial martensite softens by 15 HRC.

Find: the net hardness contributed by secondary hardening.

Assumption: the hardness of the structure is the volume-weighted sum of its constituents (rule of mixtures).

Step 1. Hardness of the initial martensite from the as-quenched state:

60 = 0.80\,H_M + 0.20(40) \;\Rightarrow\; H_M = \frac{60 - 8}{0.80} = 65\ \mathrm{HRC}

This equals the hardness of the martensite later formed from RA, as expected for the same matrix.

Step 2. Constituents after treatment, without secondary hardening:

ConstituentFractionHardness, HRCContribution, HRC
Initial martensite, tempered0.8065 - 15 = 5040.0
Martensite from RA0.20 - 0.02 = 0.186511.7
Remaining RA0.02400.8
Total1.0052.5

Step 3. Secondary hardening:

\Delta H_{SH} = 68 - 52.5 = 15.5\ \mathrm{HRC}

Check as a balance of changes:

60 + \underbrace{0.18(65 - 40)}_{+4.5} - \underbrace{0.80(15)}_{12} + \Delta H_{SH} = 68 \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta H_{SH} = 15.5\ \mathrm{HRC}

Answer: secondary hardening contributes about +15.5 HRC, about 23% of the final 68 HRC; without it the steel would have softened to 52.5 HRC.

What each term means:

  1. Cryotreatment and the tempers turn 18% RA into martensite (+4.5 HRC). The deep chill also creates dislocation sites that later nucleate fine carbides.
  2. Softening (-12 HRC): at 550^\circ\mathrm{C} carbon leaves the martensite, cementite precipitates and coarsens, and the matrix recovers.
  3. Secondary hardening (+15.5 HRC): at 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} Mo, W, V and Cr can diffuse and precipitate an ultrafine, coherent dispersion of alloy carbides (\mathrm{M_2C}, MC) on the dislocations. These replace cementite and pin dislocations, so they outweigh the softening and the net gain is +8 HRC.
  4. Three tempers: each cooling turns some RA into fresh martensite, which the next temper tempers; after the third, 2% RA and no untempered martensite remain.

This is why high-alloy tool steels are tempered at the secondary peak (about 550^\circ\mathrm{C}) and not at low temperature: they end harder than as quenched, with red hardness and almost no RA.
pts: States the rule-of-mixtures basis: hardness as the volume-weighted sum of the constituents
Back-calculates the initial martensite hardness, 65 HRC, from 60 = 0.8H_M + 0.2(40)
Tempered initial martensite at 50 HRC contributes 0.80 \times 50 = 40 HRC
Martensite from RA: fraction 0.18 (20 - 2%), contribution 11.7 HRC
Remaining 2% RA contributes 0.8 HRC
Hardness without secondary hardening: 52.5 HRC
Net secondary-hardening contribution 15.5 HRC (about 23% of 68 HRC)
Balance check: +4.5 (RA) - 12 (softening) + 15.5 = +8 HRC
Cryotreatment: RA to martensite, and dislocation sites that nucleate fine carbides
Softening of martensite at 550 degrees C: carbon loss, cementite coarsening, recovery
Secondary hardening: ultrafine coherent alloy carbides (\mathrm{M_2C}, MC of Mo, W, V, Cr) at 500 to 600 degrees C pinning dislocations
Why three tempers: the fresh martensite from each cycle is tempered by the next
2b.sketch:
• Hardness against tempering temperature (after book Fig 4.26): falling martensite-softening curve, rise from RA transformation, rise from carbide precipitation above about 500 degrees C, and the total curve with its secondary peak; mark 550 degrees C.
  • A waterfall bar chart: 60 HRC start, +4.5 (RA to martensite), -12 (softening), +15.5 (secondary hardening), 68 HRC final.
2b.src: Ch 2 Basic Heat Treatments of Steels, slides 53-55; Ch 4 Tool Steels, slides 25-29; Heat Treatment of Ferrous Alloys (course book), pp 148-150, 254-259
2b.watch:
• "Its 15 HRC hardness drop" is read as the drop of the initial martensite itself, worth 0.80 \times 15 = 12 HRC in the bulk. Read as a 15 HRC drop of the whole steel, the answer becomes 18.5 HRC; if the fresh martensite (65 HRC) is also given the 15 HRC drop, 18.2 HRC. State the reading you use.
  • Use 18% (not 20%) for the new martensite and keep the remaining 2% RA in the sum.
  • HRC is a non-linear scale, so the rule of mixtures is an estimate; it is the method this problem intends.

3a.html:
Carbon falls gradually from the surface to the core, so the case has no sharp edge and its depth depends on what is measured (slide 16):

  • Microstructural case depth: to where the etched structure can no longer be told from the core; it follows the carbon profile (about 0.30% C at its end).
  • Hardness case depth: from a hardness traverse of the hardened part; effective depth to 50 HRC, total depth to the core hardness. On slide 16: about 0.26 mm effective, 0.44 mm total by microstructure, 0.50 mm total by hardness.

Why they differ

  1. Hardness is not linear in carbon (slide 16): it rises steeply up to about 0.4% C and is flat above 0.6% C. The outer case stays near 60 to 64 HRC while carbon falls; near the core a carbon rise too small to see on etching still adds hardness.
  2. Hardness needs martensite, which depends on hardenability, section size and quench; the carbon depth depends only on time, temperature and carbon potential. A slack quench gives bainite or pearlite in the inner case and a shallower hardness depth.
  3. Retained austenite and carbides soften the high-carbon surface.
  4. Tempering lowers hardness, moving the 50 HRC point inward, but not the carbon.
pts: Defines both measures: microstructural depth on an etched section, following carbon (about 0.30% C); hardness depth from a traverse, effective to 50 HRC and total to core hardness
Reason: hardness is non-linear in carbon, flat above 0.6% C and steep at low carbon, so the two profiles do not match
Reason: hardness depends on the martensite fraction (hardenability, section, quench), the microstructural depth on carbon only
Reasons: retained austenite or carbides at the surface; tempering lowers hardness but not carbon
Sketches the carbon and hardness profiles with the depths marked and the hardness-carbon curve
3a.sketch:
• Carbon against depth: erf-shaped fall from about 0.9% at the surface to the core value, with the 0.30% C point marked "microstructural case depth".
  • Hardness against depth (slide 16): plateau, steep fall, flat core; the 50 HRC line giving the effective case depth, and the total depths by microstructure (about 440 µm) and by hardness (about 500 µm).
  • Martensite hardness against % carbon: steep to 0.4% C, flat above 0.6% C.
3a.src: Ch 3 Surface Hardening, slides 6, 16; Heat Treatment of Ferrous Alloys (course book), pp 183, 195-196; Standard textbook treatment
3a.watch:
• The depths are read from the slide 16 graph; quote them as approximate.
  • Drawings specify the effective case depth (to 50 HRC) because it measures the load-bearing case; the microstructural depth is a quick shop check on a slowly cooled sample.
  • The course book also mentions a hardness criterion of about 30 HRC for the total case; state which hardness limit you use.

3b.html:
Given (wt%): C 0.10, Si 1.30, Mn 2.60, Cr 18.6, Ni 7.00, Nb 0.05, Al 0.20; Mo and N not given (taken as 0).

Find: \mathrm{Cr_{eq}}, \mathrm{Ni_{eq}}, the type of stainless steel and its properties.

Step 1. Equivalents (Schaeffler, slide 18): ferrite formers are summed as chromium equivalent, austenite formers as nickel equivalent.

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Cr_{eq}} &= \%\mathrm{Cr} + \%\mathrm{Mo} + 1.5\,\%\mathrm{Si} + 0.5\,\%\mathrm{Nb} \\ &= 18.6 + 0 + 1.5(1.30) + 0.5(0.05) = 18.6 + 1.95 + 0.025 = 20.6 \\ \mathrm{Ni_{eq}} &= \%\mathrm{Ni} + 30\,\%\mathrm{C} + 0.5\,\%\mathrm{Mn} \\ &= 7.00 + 30(0.10) + 0.5(2.60) = 7.00 + 3.00 + 1.30 = 11.3 \end{aligned}

Step 2. Plot on Figure 1. The point (20.6, 11.3) lies inside the austenitic alloys field, above the heavy boundary line, in the A + F band. From the figure it falls between the 5% and 10% ferrite lines, almost on the 10% line: about 10% \delta-ferrite.

Answer: \mathrm{Cr_{eq}} \approx 20.6, \mathrm{Ni_{eq}} = 11.3. The steel is an austenitic stainless steel (18-8 type, like 301/302) with about 10% \delta-ferrite.

Step 3. Supporting values:

\begin{aligned} M_s &= 1302 - 42(18.6) - 61(7) - 33(2.6) - 28(1.3) - 1667(0.10) \approx -195^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ M_{d30} &= 413 - 13.7(18.6) - 9.5(7) - 8.1(2.6) - 9.2(1.3) - 462(0.10) \approx 12^\circ\mathrm{C} \end{aligned}

Unique properties:

  1. FCC matrix: high ductility and toughness, no ductile-brittle transition, excellent cryogenic toughness; nearly non-magnetic (the 10% ferrite makes it weakly magnetic).
  2. Not hardenable by heat treatment: M_s is far below room temperature. It is hardened by cold work, and with M_{d30} near room temperature (only 7% Ni) the austenite is metastable: strain-induced \alpha' gives very high work hardening.
  3. \delta-ferrite (5 to 10%) prevents hot cracking in casting and welding and raises yield strength slightly; but it can turn to sigma (600 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}) or \alpha' (near 475^\circ\mathrm{C}) and embrittle.
  4. Corrosion: 18.6% Cr gives the passive film; 1.3% Si helps scaling resistance. But 0.10% C with only 0.05% Nb is not stabilised (needs Nb at least 10 \times \mathrm{C} = 1.0\%), so it sensitises at 425 to 815^\circ\mathrm{C}; use solution annealing and quenching.
  5. Thermal: low conductivity and high expansion, so heat slowly and allow for distortion.
pts: Correct \mathrm{Cr_{eq}} formula (Cr + Mo + 1.5 Si + 0.5 Nb)
Correct \mathrm{Ni_{eq}} formula (Ni + 30 C + 0.5 Mn)
\mathrm{Cr_{eq}} = 20.6 with the substitution shown
\mathrm{Ni_{eq}} = 11.3 with the substitution shown
Point plotted on Figure 1 in the austenitic-alloy field, A + F band
Ferrite read as about 10% (between the 5% and 10% lines)
Identifies the type: austenitic stainless steel (18-8 type) with some \delta-ferrite
Property: FCC, ductile and tough to cryogenic temperatures, essentially non-magnetic
Property: not heat-treatable (M_s about -195^\circ\mathrm{C}), hardened by cold work with strain-induced martensite (M_{d30} about 12^\circ\mathrm{C})
Property: role of \delta-ferrite (hot-cracking resistance; sigma or 475 C embrittlement risk)
Property: unstabilised 0.10% C with 0.05% Nb, so sensitisation and intergranular corrosion risk; remedy named
Property: low thermal conductivity and high expansion

3b.watch:
• The ferrite percentage is read off the figure and is approximate (about 9 to 10%); the class (austenitic with some ferrite) does not depend on it.
  • Al (0.20%) is a ferrite former but is not in the Schaeffler formula printed on the slide. Counted with an extended coefficient (for example 5.5 Al), \mathrm{Cr_{eq}} \approx 21.7 and the ferrite rises to about 12 to 13%: still austenitic.
  • Use 30\,\%\mathrm{C} and 0.5\,\%\mathrm{Mn} in \mathrm{Ni_{eq}}: leaving out carbon (\mathrm{Ni_{eq}} = 8.3) drops the point below the austenitic-alloy boundary to about 25% ferrite and gives the wrong class.
  • The diagram describes the as-solidified (cast or weld) structure; it ignores cooling rate and later heat treatment.

Vacuum (low-pressure) carburising is the most eco-friendly; "peak" is read as pack.

PackGasVacuum
Carbon sourcecharcoal, coke, \mathrm{BaCO_3}endothermic gas (CO, \mathrm{H_2}, \mathrm{CH_4})small pulses of \mathrm{C_2H_2} or \mathrm{C_3H_8}
EmissionsCO, dust, spent Ba compoundCO-rich exhaust burnt off, \mathrm{CO_2}, sootessentially hydrogen; no CO or soot

Why vacuum wins:

  1. No oxygen-bearing atmosphere: no CO or toxic off-gas, no burn-off flame, no internal oxidation.
  2. Little gas: only short boost pulses; acetylene gives about 60% carbon yield (slide 10), so little is wasted.
  3. Gas quenching: no quench oil, washers or liquid waste; parts come out clean.
  4. Shorter cycles: up to about 1040^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide 9), so less energy per part.
  5. Minimum distortion: less grinding, so less material and energy; cold-to-cold, automatic.

Pack is the least green (slow, dusty, hand handling); gas is in between. The cost is high capital.

  • Plasma carburising is equally clean, but it is not one of the three options asked.

4b.html:
Choice: selective (induction) hardening of a quenched and tempered medium-carbon steel, such as AISI 1045 or 1541 for light axles and 4140 for heavy ones.

Why not carburising here. Carburising gives the hardest case (about 60 to 64 HRC), but:

  • the case is 0.8 to 1.0% C plate martensite with retained austenite, brittle under the shocks and overloads a truck axle sees;
  • the long hold at 900 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C} coarsens the grain, and the whole long axle must be quenched: distortion, straightening, cracks;
  • the case is only about 1 to 2 mm deep, and the long cycle is costly.

Why induction hardening suits a toughness-first specification

  1. Adequate, lower hardness: 0.45% C martensite gives at most 35 + 50(0.45) \approx 57 HRC, enough for splines and bearing seats.
  2. Tougher case: medium-carbon lath martensite with little retained austenite.
  3. Deep case: 3 to 8 mm (about a quarter to a third of the radius), set by frequency, carries the torsion and bending stress gradient.
  4. Compressive surface stress: the expanding martensite case is held by the unhardened core, which raises fatigue strength.
  5. Tough core: keeps its quenched and tempered structure (about 25 to 30 HRC) and absorbs the shocks.
  6. Short local heating: no grain growth, little distortion, no atmosphere, only the needed zones, in-line and cheap per part.

Process design

  • Prior treatment: quench and temper, giving a fine uniform structure that austenitises in seconds.
  • Frequency: \delta = 5.03\sqrt{\rho/(\mu f)} cm (slide 38). Above the Curie point \mu = 1 and \rho \approx 115\ \mu\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}, so 3 kHz gives \delta \approx 1.0 cm and 10 kHz about 0.54 cm: use 1 to 10 kHz for a 3 to 8 mm case.
  • Scan hardening: the rotating axle passes through the coil, the surface reaches about 900 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} (fast heating raises \mathrm{Ac_3}; book p 132), and a following water or polymer spray quenches it.
  • Temper at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} to about 52 to 55 HRC.

Microstructure, surface to core

  1. Case: fine, low-tempered lath martensite, 52 to 57 HRC.
  2. Transition zone (heated between \mathrm{Ac_1} and \mathrm{Ac_3}): martensite with undissolved ferrite or over-tempered martensite; hardness falls steeply.
  3. Core: unaffected tempered martensite (sorbite), or ferrite + pearlite if normalised, about 25 to 30 HRC.

A carburised axle would instead show high-carbon martensite with retained austenite, then a hypoeutectoid transition, then low-carbon lath martensite or ferrite + bainite.

Conclusion: induction hardening meets the toughness-first specification at lower cost.
pts: Chooses selective (induction) hardening of a named medium-carbon steel (1045, 1541 or 4140)
Argues against carburising: brittle high-carbon plate martensite with retained austenite, grain growth and distortion of a long axle in a long hot cycle, shallow case and cost
Case of about 0.45% C martensite: about 55 to 57 HRC, lower but adequate, tougher, little retained austenite
Deep case (3 to 8 mm) and compressive surface stress raise torsional and bending fatigue strength

Plan (Grossmann method):

  1. Machine round bars of several diameters (for example 1/2, 3/4, 1, 1 1/2 and 2 in) from the plate, each at least four diameters long so the mid-length is free of end cooling.
  2. Austenitise them together above A_3 (910 - 203\sqrt{0.3} - 15.2(3.2) + 44.7(0.8) \approx 786^\circ\mathrm{C}), at about 830^\circ\mathrm{C}, soaking 60 + D min.
  3. Quench all in brine with violent agitation, H = 5.0 (Table 2).
  4. Section each bar at mid-length; measure HRC along the diameter and the martensite fraction at the centre by image analysis.
  5. The 50% martensite hardness for 0.30% C is 23 + 50(0.30) = 38 HRC. Smaller bars stay above it at the centre; larger bars show a soft U-shaped core. The diameter whose centre has exactly 50% martensite is the critical diameter D.

Reasonable value: in Figure 2 the 1 in bar just touches the 50% M line at its centre, so D = 1.0 in (25 mm).

D_I: on Figure 3, go across at D = 1.0 in to the H = 5.0 curve and down:

Answer: D_I \approx 1.2 in (about 30 mm).

Neither: D_I stays the same. D_I is the diameter that gives 50% martensite at the centre in an ideal quench (H = \infty), which brings the surface to the bath temperature in zero time. It removes the quenchant from the definition and depends only on the steel: dissolved carbon and alloy, and austenite grain size.

What the medium changes is the critical diameter D, through the severity H. For this steel (D_I \approx 1.2 in), Figure 3 gives:

A milder medium lowers D and a more severe one raises it, but each (D, H) pair reads back to the same D_I; any spread is experimental error.

Step 2. Base value for 0.30% C, grain size 7 (Figure 4): D_{I,\mathrm{base}} \approx 0.18 in (4.6 mm).

Step 3. Multiplying factors (Figure 5):

5iv.html:
Yes, a large difference. From carbon and grain size alone (Figure 4), D_I \approx 0.18 in (4.6 mm); with all the elements (Figure 5), D_I \approx 0.18 \times 3.65 \times 1.55 \times 2.8 \times 3.6 \approx 10 in, about 57 times larger.

Reasons:

  1. The base value describes a plain Fe-C alloy. Carbon delays ferrite and pearlite only slightly, and fine grains (ASTM 7) give many nucleation sites, so it is tiny.
  2. Dissolved alloying elements slow the diffusional reactions. Ferrite and pearlite need Mn, Ni, Cr and Si to redistribute by slow substitutional diffusion; solutes also drag the interface. The TTT nose shifts right, the critical cooling rate falls, and thicker bars reach 50% martensite at the centre.
  3. The effects multiply: each element stretches the incubation time by its own factor. Here Mn (3.65) and Cr (3.6) are strongest, then Ni (2.8) and Si (1.55).
  4. Conditions: only dissolved elements count (undissolved Cr carbides add nothing), for low and medium carbon steels; Co lowers hardenability.

Conclusion: the alloy, not the carbon, governs this steel's hardenability.

6a.html:
Test design (end-quench, Jominy and Boegehold)

  1. Specimen: 25 mm (1 in) diameter, 100 mm (4 in) long, with a collar at the top for hanging; machined below any decarburised skin.
  2. Normalise first at about 925^\circ\mathrm{C}, air cool, so every heat starts from the same structure.
  3. Austenitise at 925^\circ\mathrm{C} for 30 min. For 0.15% C, A_3 \approx 860^\circ\mathrm{C} (Fe-Fe3C diagram; 910 - 203\sqrt{0.15} \approx 831^\circ\mathrm{C} by Andrews), and low-carbon steels are tested at this higher standard temperature. Protect the bar (inert gas, or a graphite disc on the end face) against scaling and decarburisation.
  4. Quench within 5 s in the fixture: a water jet (12.7 mm orifice, 63.5 mm free height, water 5 to 30^\circ\mathrm{C}) hits only the lower face, for at least 10 min.
  5. Measure: grind two opposite flats about 0.45 mm deep; take HRC every 1/16 in (about 2 mm) from the quenched end, then wider; for this shallow-hardening steel add readings every 1/32 in over the first 1/4 in. Below 20 HRC, record HRB.

Expected curve (0.15% C)

Maximum possible: \mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} = 35 + 50(0.15) = 42.5; 50% martensite: 23 + 50(0.15) = 30.5 HRC. Plain 0.15% C steel (D_I \approx 0.3 in) has its nose below 1 s, so even the end is not fully martensitic: about 35 to 40 HRC at the face, about 30 HRC near 1/16 in, below 20 HRC by about 1/4 in, then a flat ferrite + pearlite level (about 80 to 85 HRB) to the far end.

Industrial significance

  • Each distance has a fixed cooling rate at 700^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 270, 70, 18 and 5.6^\circ\mathrm{C/s} at 1/16, 4/16, 8/16 and 16/16 in), whatever the steel, so one cheap, reproducible bar gives hardness against cooling rate.
  • It fixes hardenability bands of H-steels for purchase and heat acceptance, and gives D_I from the 50% martensite distance.
  • This plot shows a shallow-hardening steel: a carburising grade whose Jominy curve gives the core hardness.

Choosing a grade

  1. Find the as-quenched hardness needed at the critical point: 35 HRC after tempering at 500^\circ\mathrm{C} needs 45 HRC (book Fig 2.41), or 80% martensite with 0.37% C gives 45 HRC.
  2. Convert that point to a Jominy distance with equal cooling rate: 3/4 radius of a 45 mm shaft, oil quenched, equals 13/32 in.
  3. Choose the cheapest grade whose minimum band curve meets it there: 4140H gives at least 49 HRC at 13/32 in, so it qualifies; the 0.15% C steel (below 20 HRC there) does not.

6b.html:
Three cooling stages, whenever the quenchant is a liquid that boils (water, brine, oil, polymer). The number is fixed by the boiling of the quenchant, not by the 0.47% C; the carbon decides where the steel's transformations fall on these stages.

  1. Stage A, vapour blanket (film boiling). An unbroken vapour film insulates the part; heat leaves only by conduction and radiation through it: slow cooling. In oil it ends near 690^\circ\mathrm{C}, when the film collapses.
  2. Stage B, nucleate (bubble) boiling. Liquid wets the surface and boils violently; the heat of vaporisation gives the fastest cooling (about 95^\circ\mathrm{C/s} near 600^\circ\mathrm{C} in oil). It ends at the boiling point, about 315^\circ\mathrm{C} for oil. Most distortion arises here.
  3. Stage C, convection. Below the boiling point heat leaves by convection and conduction only: the slowest stage, governed by viscosity and bath temperature.

Validation for 0.47% C (AISI 1045 class): the pearlite nose (about 550^\circ\mathrm{C}, under 1 s) must be passed during stage B, and

M_s = 520 - 320(0.47) - 50(0.75) \approx 330^\circ\mathrm{C}

In oil, stage C starts near M_s, so martensite forms under slow cooling and stresses equalise. In water, stage B lasts to about 100 to 150^\circ\mathrm{C}, through the martensite range, so distortion and cracking risks are higher.
pts: States three stages for a boiling liquid quenchant, set by the quenchant and not by the carbon content
Stage A: continuous vapour film insulates the part; slow cooling by conduction and radiation through the vapour
Stage B: film collapses, violent nucleate boiling, fastest cooling by heat of vaporisation, ends at the boiling point; most distortion
Stage C: convection and conduction below the boiling point, slowest, controlled by viscosity and bath temperature
Diagrams: tank sketch and cooling and cooling-rate curves with the three bands, related to the steel's nose and M_s \approx 330^\circ\mathrm{C} (oil reaches stage C near Ms, water does not)

7a.html:
Austempering. It produces the final structure and properties in one step. Martempering (marquenching) only controls distortion: it still gives brittle untempered martensite that must be tempered, so the properties are those of ordinary quenching and tempering.

Why martempering adds little at 0.14% C. Its benefit is a small surface-centre gradient while martensite forms. This steel forms soft lath martensite (at most 35 + 50(0.14) = 42 HRC) at a high M_s = 520 - 320(0.14) - 50(0.4) \approx 455^\circ\mathrm{C}, so quench stresses are small anyway, and a hold just above M_s falls inside the bainite and ferrite region of such a lean steel.

Austempering cycle: austenitise at about 900^\circ\mathrm{C} (A_3 \approx 860^\circ\mathrm{C}); quench into a violently agitated salt bath between M_s and B_s = 630 - 45(0.4) - 35(0.2) \approx 605^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 470 to 500^\circ\mathrm{C}; hold until transformation is complete; air cool. No tempering.

Factors that give the properties

  1. Bainitic structure: fine bainitic ferrite laths with fine carbide. Small lath size and dislocations give strength; no brittle martensite and little carbide (0.14% C) give toughness.
  2. Complete isothermal transformation: holding to the finish line (curve C, slide 67) gives 100% bainite; short holds (curves A, B) leave austenite that becomes fresh martensite on cooling.
  3. Bath temperature: just above M_s gives the finest, strongest bainite; above B_s, soft ferrite and pearlite form.
  4. Uniform structure and hardness: surface and core transform at the same temperature.
  5. Low residual stress, little distortion, no quench cracks: thermal contraction ends in hot, plastic austenite and the transformation is isothermal.
  6. Better ductility, impact and fatigue strength than quenched and tempered martensite of equal hardness: no microcracks, no tempered-martensite embrittlement range.
  7. Less hydrogen embrittlement and a clean, scale-free surface from the neutral salt (plater friendly).
  8. No tempering step: shorter, cheaper cycle.
  9. Hardenability and section size: 0.14% C has a ferrite nose well under 1 s, so only thin sections (slide 68: 0.008 to 0.150 in, 0.2 to 3.8 mm) or grades with Mn, Cr, Mo or B reach the bath untransformed.

Conclusion: austempering, for thin sections or a slightly alloyed 0.14% C grade.

7b.html:
P is a cheap and powerful strengthener (0.17% P adds about 62 MPa to YS and UTS), yet in general carbon steels (structural sections, rebar, forgings, welded and heat-treated parts) it is held below about 0.04%, because:

  1. It buys strength with toughness. Solid-solution strengthening by P raises the ductile-brittle transition temperature sharply: cold shortness. Grain refinement, by contrast, raises strength and toughness together.
  2. Grain-boundary segregation. P segregates to grain boundaries and lowers their cohesion, so brittle fracture changes from transgranular cleavage to intergranular (slide 26).
  3. Temper embrittlement. In quenched and tempered steels P, helped by Mn and Ni, segregates to prior-austenite boundaries during tempering or slow cooling through about 375 to 575^\circ\mathrm{C}, and impact toughness collapses.
  4. Segregation in casting. P diffuses slowly and segregates strongly on freezing; P-rich bands become banded ferrite (ghost lines), so properties are uneven and cold working needs a careful rolling schedule.
  5. Processing problems. Above 0.04% P galvanised coatings are rough and brittle; P aids weld cracking, and reheated deep-drawn sheet suffers secondary work embrittlement.

General carbon steels are chosen for toughness, ductility, weldability and reliability rather than maximum strength, so the small strength gain is not worth the risk; strength comes from C, Mn and grain refinement instead. P is added deliberately only in special grades: rephosphorised sheet, weathering and free-cutting steels.

7c.html:
Vanadium. It is a microalloying element (0.03 to 0.15% is enough). Fine V(C,N) precipitates strengthen the ferrite, and pinning of austenite grain boundaries in controlled rolling gives fine ferrite grains, so strength and toughness rise together. With 100 to 150 ppm N, about 0.1% V adds roughly 140 to 170 MPa to the yield strength (book Fig. 1.85).

Mn at 0.5% gives only mild solid-solution strengthening (about 30 MPa per 1% Mn) and some pearlite refinement.

Cu has low solubility in ferrite; below 0.75% it does not age harden, generally lowers tensile strength (slide 48) and risks hot shortness.

8a.html:
Given: low-carbon steel plate, 50 \times 120 \times 4 mm. Assumed: AISI 1020 (0.20% C, 0.45% Mn).

Find: full-annealing and normalising schedules.

Critical temperatures (Fe-Fe3C diagram, slide 10): \mathrm{A_3} \approx 845^\circ\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{A_1} = 727^\circ\mathrm{C}. The 4 mm thickness controls heating and cooling.

Heating (both): the carbon equivalent is well below 0.4 and the plate is thin, so it can be charged into the hot furnace.

Full annealing

\begin{aligned} T &= \mathrm{A_3} + (30\ \text{to}\ 40) = 875\ \text{to}\ 885^\circ\mathrm{C}, \quad \text{take } 880^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ t_{\text{soak}} &\geq 20\ \mathrm{min\,cm^{-1}} \times 0.4\ \mathrm{cm} = 8\ \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}

Hold about 10 min once the plate is at temperature. Furnace cool at 20 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}} to below \mathrm{A_1}, about 650^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 7.7 h at 30^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}), then air cool. Result: coarse ferrite + about 23% coarse pearlite,

\mathrm{UTS} \approx 0.774(40{,}000) + 0.226(120{,}000) = 58{,}100\ \mathrm{psi} \approx 400\ \mathrm{MPa}, \quad \mathrm{YS} \approx \mathrm{UTS}/1.5 \approx 267\ \mathrm{MPa}

Normalising

\begin{aligned} T &= \mathrm{A_3} + (50\ \text{to}\ 60) = 895\ \text{to}\ 905^\circ\mathrm{C}, \quad \text{take } 900^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ t_{\text{hold}} &= 60 + D = 60 + 4 = 64\ \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}

Cool in still air, with the plate on edge or on a grid so both faces cool alike and it does not warp. Result: finer ferrite and pearlite, slightly stronger and harder than the annealed plate.

Answer: anneal 880^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 10 min, furnace cool to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} then air; normalise 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 1 h, still air.

8b.html:
Significance of austenitising. It is the first and most decisive step of hardening (and of full annealing and normalising):

  • Only FCC austenite dissolves enough carbon (up to 2.14%, against 0.022% in ferrite). The dissolved carbon and alloy fix the martensite hardness (\mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} = 35 + 50\%\mathrm{C}), the hardenability and M_s.
  • It sets the austenite grain size and homogeneity, hence toughness, distortion and the uniformity of hardening.
  • It takes time: incubation, then growth, then carbon equalisation (0.8% C steel: at 730^\circ\mathrm{C} it starts after about 30 s; at 750^\circ\mathrm{C} it starts in 10 s and ends in 50 s; carbides take longer). Soak about 60 + D min. Faster heating raises \mathrm{Ac_1} and \mathrm{Ac_3}.
  • Too low or too short leaves soft ferrite and undissolved carbides; too high gives grain growth, retained austenite, decarburisation and cracking.

Nucleus formation on heating:

  • Hypoeutectoid steel (ferrite + pearlite): above \mathrm{Ac_1}, nuclei form at the intersections of pearlite colonies and on the cementite lamellae; several grains grow from each colony. On further heating the austenite grows into the proeutectoid ferrite, fed by carbon diffusing from the former pearlite, until \mathrm{Ac_3}.
  • Ferritic steel: nuclei form at the ferrite grain boundaries, mainly triple junctions, and spread along the boundaries.
pts: Austenite dissolves carbon; dissolved C and alloy set martensite hardness, hardenability and M_s
Controls austenite grain size and homogeneity, hence properties and uniform hardening
Time and temperature: incubation and growth (30 s start at 730 degrees C, 10 to 50 s at 750 degrees C), soak 60 + D; heating rate raises Ac1 and Ac3
Consequences of under- and over-austenitising

8d.html:
How it is obtained. Retained austenite (RA) remains when the quench ends above M_f:

  • More than about 0.65% C, or Mn, Cr, Ni, Cu, puts M_f below room temperature.
  • A higher austenitising temperature dissolves more carbon and carbide, lowering M_s.
  • Holding or slow cooling below M_s stabilises austenite.

Why it is detrimental.

  • RA is soft FCC austenite: above about 10% it lowers hardness, strength and wear resistance markedly.
  • It is unstable: with time or stress it becomes untempered, brittle martensite with a volume increase, causing distortion and cracking in service.
pts: RA is austenite left when the quench ends above Mf; Mf is below room temperature for more than about 0.65% C and for alloyed steels
A high austenitising temperature (more dissolved C and alloy) and holding or slow cooling below Ms increase RA
RA is soft: hardness, strength and wear resistance fall, markedly above about 10%
RA is unstable: it later forms untempered martensite with expansion, giving dimensional instability and cracking

  • A one-line remedy earns goodwill: cold or cryogenic treatment (-70 to -196^\circ\mathrm{C}) before tempering, or multiple tempers.

8e.html:
Carbon lowers M_s (about 430^\circ\mathrm{C} at 0.2% C, 200^\circ\mathrm{C} at 1.0% C) and strengthens the austenite, which changes how the shear is accommodated:

  • Below about 0.5 to 0.6% C: lath (massive) martensite. At high M_s the shear is accommodated by slip: thin parallel laths in packets, high dislocation density.
  • 0.6 to 1.0% C: laths and plates mixed.
  • Above about 1.0% C: plate (needle) martensite. At low M_s twinning takes over: twinned plates at angles to one another, limited by the austenite grain, with retained austenite.

Tetragonality also rises, c/a \approx 1 + 0.045(\%\mathrm{C}): harder, more brittle martensite.
pts: States that carbon lowers Ms and strengthens the austenite
Low carbon (below about 0.5 to 0.6%): lath martensite in packets, dislocated substructure, slip
High carbon (above about 1.0%): plate or needle martensite, twinned, limited by the austenite grain
